title: Dvaita and beyond (Madhva, Ramanuja): the lover and the beloved stay two; why devotion needs difference (6 of 7)
hook: a devotee is kept outside a temple wall, and the story says the image of Krishna turned around to face him
carry: two, and the space between is love
tomorrow: Dvaita and beyond (7 of 7): why devotion needs difference

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dvaita and beyond, part five: taking refuge, and the baby monkey and the kitten, both held. Did you let someone help you? Today, Madhva. Day two hundred ninety-three.

Udupi, on the coast of Karnataka. There's a famous temple of Krishna there, and in its western wall there's a small window. People line up to look through it. Here's the story they tell about it. About five hundred years ago, a poet named Kanakadasa came to worship. He was from a community that wasn't allowed inside. So he stood outside the back wall and sang to Krishna, for hours, in his own language. And the story says the wall cracked, and the image of Krishna inside turned around to face him. That window is still called Kanaka's window. The temple was founded by the teacher we meet today.
screen: `A TEMPLE IN UDUPI.` → `A POET OUTSIDE THE WALL.` → `KANAKA'S WINDOW.`

segments.voice: His name was Madhva, and tradition places him in the thirteenth century. He taught the school now called Dvaita, which means two. Madhva himself called it tattvavada: the teaching of what is real. His claim is simple and bold. God is real. You are real. The world is real. And they are different, forever. He listed five differences that never go away. God is different from souls. God is different from matter. Souls are different from matter. Each soul is different from every other soul. And each piece of matter is different from every other piece. Five walls, you could say, that never come down. That sounds cold, until you see why he wanted it. For Madhva, if the soul is secretly God, then worship is a kind of pretending. But if God is truly other, truly greater, then love has somewhere to go. His followers sum it up in a phrase: Hari sarvottama, Vishnu is supreme. And every soul, however humble, depends on him and can turn to him. Now back to the window. Kanakadasa stood on the far side of a real wall, the kind people build, and the story says God turned toward him. It isn't a story about Madhva's philosophy exactly. It's a story his tradition loves, and it carries the same shape: a real distance, and a love that crosses it. The Advaita teachers you met earlier would say the distance is finally unreal. Madhva's followers say the distance is where love lives. Both are Hindu, and both are still taught.
screen: `MADHVA: THE TEACHING OF WHAT IS REAL.` · `FIVE DIFFERENCES THAT NEVER GO AWAY.` · `IF GOD IS OTHER, LOVE HAS A PLACE TO GO.` · `A REAL DISTANCE, AND A LOVE THAT CROSSES IT.` · then, large: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let yourself feel small for a moment, in a good way. Not ashamed. Just small, the way you feel under a big sky. Breathe in, and notice how much is bigger than you: the day ahead, the people you love, whatever holds it all. Breathe out, and let the distance be fine. Kanakadasa sang from outside the wall. If you pray, you can turn toward God from exactly where you are. If you don't, just face toward something larger, and rest. The bell holds the time.
Dvaita and beyond, part six. Madhva's Dvaita: God, souls and the world are real, and different forever. The distance isn't a problem to solve. It's where love goes.
Your line: two, and the space between is love. Today, notice someone standing outside a wall, at work, at school, at the edge of a group, and turn toward them. Day two hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Followers of Madhva, often called Madhvas, worship Vishnu as supreme; the Krishna temple at Udupi, which tradition says Madhva founded, is their great center, and pilgrims still look through Kanaka's window.

original.note: Sanskrit: two-ness, duality, from dvi, two. The name later given to Madhva's school; he called it tattvavada.

trapdoor: what you thought: dvaita means dualism, like good against evil.
what it means: God, souls and the world are all real and forever distinct, and souls depend on God.
what a scholar hears: pancha-bheda, the five differences. Madhva named his school tattvavada, the doctrine of reality; 'dvaita' is the label others gave it.
